Practices with unfamiliar names, in plain words

You sit with a single point of light — a candle, or a dot on the wall — and keep your eyes there. When your attention drifts you bring it back. That\'s the whole practice. It settles a busy mind faster than most breathing work, and it\'s the one to reach for when thoughts won\'t stop moving.
Works best in a dim room

You lie on your back and a voice moves your attention through the body, one part at a time. You are not trying to sleep, though many people do. Twenty minutes of it leaves most people feeling like they napped for an hour.
You sit and notice whatever shows up — the breath, a sound, an ache, a thought — without chasing or pushing it away. Older and plainer than it sounds, and the base most other practices are built on.

You repeat a handful of simple wishes: may I be well, may I be at ease. Then you send the same lines to someone you love, someone neutral, someone difficult. It\'s the practice for days when you\'re being hard on yourself.
Repeating phrases, not clearing the mind
Feeling nothing at first is normal

You inhale normally, then hum through a long exhale with your mouth closed, like a soft engine. You repeat this several times in a row. The sound fills your head just enough to turn the thoughts down.
Inhale in silence, then hum on the exhale
It repeats several rounds in a row
It doesn\'t need to sound \"good\", the hum is enough

Sitting with a straight back, you exhale sharp and short through the nose, over and over, letting the inhale happen passively between exhales. It\'s done in rounds, with a rest between each one. This is active, not relaxed — you\'ll feel your belly working.
The inhale is passive, the effort is in the exhale
There\'s a rest between each round

It opens with a bell, a short posture cue — straight back, still hands — then silence, no spoken guidance or music. It closes with another bell. There\'s no special breathing technique or anything to visualize: just posture and time seated.
Opens and closes with a bell
The middle is total silence, no voice guiding you

On each inhale you think (or whisper) the syllable \"So\", and on each exhale \"Hum\". It repeats like that, breath after breath, for the whole session. There\'s nothing to understand or translate — it\'s just a simple anchor for the mind while you breathe.
\"So\" goes with the inhale, \"Hum\" with the exhale
You can think it, whisper it, or say it out loud
It repeats the whole time, it doesn\'t change
Repeating a phrase, out loud or silently
You set an intention, then repeat a short phrase — your own, or one you pick — a fixed number of times (11, 33, or 99). It ends in silence. The app counts the repetitions, but you choose the phrase.
You choose (or write) the phrase you repeat
You can say it aloud, under your breath, or just think it
It ends in silence, no spoken closing

It opens with a moment to set an intention, then a stretch to settle into your breath, then an extended silence for contemplation — no guidance, no phrases to repeat. It\'s closer to zazen\'s silence than to a guided meditation.
Most of the session is unguided silence
It opens with a brief intention and breath-settling, not straight into silence
No phrases to repeat, nothing to visualize
Talking to God in your own words

After a moment to arrive, the session offers you topics — gratitude, worries, requests, relationships, purpose, forgiveness, whichever you pick — and for each one you speak in your own words, like a conversation. It ends with a stretch of free personal prayer and silence.
You speak out loud, not silently or in writing
There\'s no fixed phrase to repeat, you improvise
You choose which topics to cover before you start
Reading a sacred text in four steps

It\'s done in four steps with a text you choose and bring yourself (the app doesn\'t provide one): first you read it slowly without analyzing it, then you reflect on what stood out, then you respond to God in your own words, and it ends in silent contemplation. Each step has its own time.
You need your own text ready before you start
The first three steps have spoken guidance, the last one is silence
No need to analyze the text, just notice what stands out
